summary: Outlines possible TCP enhancements that could help it use available bandwidth better on networks that include satellite links. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Satellites are far away, so messages take a long trip. This lists ways to help TCP work well despite the delay.

questions: how to improve tcp for satellites
what are satellite link challenges for tcp
subtitle: Research into TCP mechanisms that improve performance over satellite links.

tldr.problem: Satellite links have very high latency and sometimes high bandwidth, causing TCP to operate inefficiently. Standard TCP's slow start, congestion control, and ACK handling were designed for low-latency wired networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2760 surveys ongoing research into TCP enhancements for satellite networks, including larger initial windows, modified slow start, selective acknowledgements, loss detection improvements, pacing mechanisms, header compression, and state sharing among connections.
tldr.outcome: The research community is actively investigating these mechanisms. Some, like larger initial windows and selective acknowledgements, are now standards. Others remain experimental, pending further study and deployment experience.

today: RFC 2760 is informational. Published in February 2000, it documents research that was ongoing at that time. Some mechanisms discussed (larger initial windows, selective acknowledgements) became standards. Others remain experimental or research proposals. The RFC itself is not a standard and makes no recommendations for deployment.

sections.title: Introduction: TCP Over Satellites
sections.content:
Satellite links present a unique challenge for TCP. Unlike wired networks, satellites have extremely high latency—200 milliseconds or more for geosynchronous satellites, or 24+ milliseconds for low-earth orbit satellites. Some satellite systems also have high bandwidth, making them "long fat networks," while others have low bandwidth, making them "long thin networks."

This RFC documents research mechanisms being studied to help TCP perform better over these environments. Unlike RFC 2757, which recommends specific mechanisms for wireless WANs, RFC 2760 is purely informational: it surveys proposals that are still under investigation and are not yet mature enough to be recommended by the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: Satellite links are super far away, so it takes a long time for a message to go up to the satellite and come back down. Engineers are studying many different ways to help TCP work better despite this delay.

sections.title: Satellite Network Architectures
sections.content:
Satellite links can be deployed in several ways:

Asymmetric networks: The forward link (downlink to users) has higher capacity than the return link (uplink), because of antenna and power limitations. This causes problems for TCP, which relies on relatively balanced bidirectional communication.

Satellite as last hop: The satellite link provides direct service to end users, often with a shared high-speed downlink and lower-speed terrestrial return link.

Hybrid networks: Satellite links are just one part of a larger network topology, potentially mixed with terrestrial links.

Point-to-point and multi-hop: Private satellite networks or networks with multiple satellite hops pose different challenges than shared systems.

Each architecture affects which TCP mechanisms are most appropriate and where changes can be made (sender, receiver, or intermediate nodes).
sections.plainLanguage: Satellites can be used in different ways: some have fast download but slow upload, some connect directly to users, some are part of a bigger network. Each setup needs different fixes.

sections.title: Mechanisms Under Investigation
sections.content:
Slow Start Enhancements: Larger initial congestion windows (RFC 2581 allows 2 segments, proposals suggest up to 4) reduce the time wasted during startup. Byte counting (counting data bytes, not just ACK arrivals) helps the window grow faster. Disabling delayed ACKs during slow start provides more rapid feedback from the receiver.

Loss Recovery: Selective Acknowledgements (SACK) help the sender identify exactly which segments were lost, enabling faster recovery from burst errors. Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) distinguishes corruption loss from congestion loss. Some proposals use explicit loss notification from the network to help the sender.

Pacing: Sending segments at a steady rate instead of in bursts reduces loss and queue buildup. Research suggests various pacing algorithms.

Header Compression: Compressing TCP and IP headers reduces overhead. Van Jacobson compression is standard; newer IPHC schemes are more robust.

State Sharing: Remembering connection parameters (RTT, MSS, etc.) from previous connections to the same server and reusing them in new connections saves time and improves fairness.

ACK Control: Filtering excess ACKs or shaping ACK flow can prevent ACK congestion on the return path, especially important in asymmetric networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Send more data at first. Count bytes instead of just counting responses. Receivers should answer immediately at the start. The sender should know exactly which pieces got lost. Send data at a steady rate. Squeeze the headers. Remember what worked last time. Control the flow of responses back to the sender.

sections.title: Cautions and Ongoing Research
sections.content:
This RFC emphasizes that none of these mechanisms have been judged mature enough for standardization. Some are safe to use today (like larger initial windows), while others require further study. Key concerns include:

Safety in shared networks: Aggressive mechanisms like unlimited byte counting could harm overall Internet stability if deployed widely without sufficient study. Limited byte counting is safer but still experimental.

Interactions: Some mechanisms interact badly with others. Byte counting during slow start negates the benefit of disabling delayed ACKs, because if each ACK only covers one segment, both approaches yield the same window growth.

Topology constraints: Some mechanisms only help in specific architectures (e.g., asymmetric networks or point-to-point links) and may hurt performance elsewhere.

Deployment barriers: The RFC stresses that mechanisms requiring changes at both sender and receiver are harder to deploy in real networks where legacy systems cannot be modified.
sections.plainLanguage: These are ideas, not yet proven. Some are probably okay to use. Others might break the Internet if everyone uses them. Some tricks work against each other. What works on a satellite might not work on a regular network. And it is hard to change both ends of a connection.

sections.title: Ongoing Work
sections.content:
RFC 2760 is a snapshot of ongoing research as of February 2000. The document explicitly states that these mechanisms are "not mature enough to be recommended for widespread use by the IETF." However, it serves as a research agenda: if mechanisms prove to be safe and appropriate through further study, appropriate IETF documents will be written to recommend them.

The RFC acknowledges that non-TCP mitigations (application-level changes, link-layer improvements, queueing discipline changes) also exist but are beyond the document's scope. It also mentions that gateway-based optimizations (intermediate nodes along the path) are not deeply analyzed.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a list of things researchers are studying. Some might become official standards later if they work well. But right now, none of them are recommended for everyone to use.
